ext.title: Introduction To Monte Carlo Simulation
ext.venue: AIP Conference Proceedings 1204:17-21 (published 2010 Jan 5; PMC author manuscript, available 2011). Metadata hint confirmed.
ext.document_type: Tutorial and history review paper in a conference proceedings volume (single author, Dept. of Radiology, University of Washington). Not empirical.
ext.coverage: Full text read: all of the extraction (378 lines), covering title, abstract, Introduction, History, Monte Carlo method, RNGs, inversion, acceptance-rejection, approximation, normal and Poisson sampling, tallying, Summary, Acknowledgments, references 1-14, and captions for Figures 1-7. Figure images and equation bodies (eqs. 1-8) are not in the text extraction, so their content is not verified. Paul's markup: all 31 highlights in the annotation JSON read. Highlights cluster on pp.1-3 and p.6, with one on p.4; none on pp.4-5 inversion, acceptance-rejection or Poisson derivations except the library-function advice. Two highlight colours; the green one is the 'Key points' line on p.2. Quotes limited to one under the copyright rule; markup text is paraphrased, not reproduced.
ext.research_question: What Monte Carlo simulation is, where it came from, and how to build one: defining a model as probability density functions, generating random numbers, sampling from standard distributions (uniform, exponential, normal, Poisson), and tallying results. Stated scope: an overview with emphasis on techniques used in medical imaging simulation.
ext.theory: No substantive theory beyond the generic Monte Carlo recipe the paper gives: model a system as probability density functions, sample repeatedly from them, tally statistics of interest. The paper states there is no single Monte Carlo method. It also cites the central limit theorem to justify normal approximation.
ext.data: No empirical dataset. Illustrative examples only: Buffon's needle (p.1, p.8 Fig.1); a qualitative weather-forecast example (p.3); exponential, normal and Poisson sampling. Sample, unit, period and N: not applicable.
ext.method: Narrative review and tutorial. No estimation, no statistical test, no simulation run. Covers: the three-step pattern (p.2); PDF/CDF requirements (p.3); pseudo-RNGs, with LCG (eq. 3) and Mersenne Twister (p.4); inversion method, exemplified by exponential sampling (eqs. 4-6, p.5); acceptance-rejection with steps 1-5 (p.5); piecewise-linear table approximation (p.5); normal sampling via CLT and library routines (pp.5-6); Poisson sampling by counting exponential inter-arrival draws (eq. 8, p.6); tallying recorded events (p.6).
ext.identification: Not applicable. Metadata hint (title, author, 2010, AIP Conf Proc 1204:17-21, DOI 10.1063/1.3295638) matches the paper's own title block and PMC stamp.
ext.scope: Population: none (methods paper). Institution: University of Washington Radiology (single author). Era: 18th-century precursors (Buffon, 1707-1788) through the 19th-century statistical examples, the WWII Manhattan Project, and modern simulation. Field emphasis: medical imaging, though the methods are general.

key_findings.finding: Buffon's needle: for a needle the same length as the line spacing, the probability of intersecting a line is 2/pi. Repeated tosses estimate pi as 2N/X, where X is the number of intersections.
Systematic Monte Carlo was developed during the Manhattan Project by von Neumann and Ulam, to study neutron travel through radiation shielding; the method is named after the Monte Carlo Casino.

Pre-modern simulation examples: De Forest (card deck, mortality tables, 1834-1888); G.H. Darwin (spinner, curve smoothing, 1845-1912); Galton (modified dice for a normal distribution, 1822-1911); Gosset/'Student' (labelled cards, t-test, 1876-1937). Paper calls them seminal but distinct from modern simulation, which solves deterministic problems probabilistically.

Simulation drawbacks: it can need huge computing resources, gives no exact solutions, is only as good as the model and inputs, and is prone to software bugs. The author says analytic and experimental alternatives should be considered first.
Weather example: forecasts are more accurate in densely sampled regions (many stations, satellites, balloons) than near poorly sampled regions, so input measurement limits prediction.
A PDF must be non-negative and integrate to 1. The CDF gives the probability that a sampled value is at most x (eq. 2; equation body not extracted).

Most RNGs sample integers 0..N and divide by N to get [0,1). Linear congruential generators are old and do poorly on Diehard-type tests. Mersenne Twister is 'rapidly becoming the generator of choice', passing most tests except those aimed at encryption RNGs.
Inversion method: draw u uniform on [0,1) and invert the CDF. Exponential sampling is the worked case (eqs. 4-6). The method works for any distribution with an invertible CDF.
Acceptance-rejection is an exact method (not an approximation). It needs two uniform draws per accepted sample. Accept v when c*u <= f(v)/g(v); on average c iterations are needed.
key_findings.numbers: c iterations on average; 2 uniforms per sample

key_findings.finding: Piecewise-linear table approximation with interpolation can be among the fastest samplers, but it adds bias. Removing the bias with acceptance-rejection costs an extra uniform draw, which often cancels the speed gain.

Normal distribution: the CLT is given as the justification for approximating unknown distributions by normals, though it only holds in the limit. The CDF has no simple inverse, so the paper recommends fast acceptance-rejection library routines.

Poisson sampling can count exponential inter-arrival draws until their sum exceeds the period; the count is the number of draws minus one. The author calls this slow and recommends a library routine. The Poisson mean and variance are both lambda.
Tallying: each event is recorded by its properties, and the process is repeated. A single event may sample many PDFs and be tallied in many ways.

measures: None. The paper's constructs are PDFs, CDFs, PMFs, RNG output, acceptance ratios and tallies. It reports no outcome measures.
limitations: No single definition of Monte Carlo; any definition omits valid cases (p.2).
Simulation needs large computing resources, gives no exact solutions, depends on model and input quality, and software can have bugs (p.2).
Simulation may be overused as a shortcut instead of analytic or experimental work (p.2).
Pseudo-random generators only mimic randomness; LCGs do poorly on standard tests; Mersenne Twister fails some encryption-oriented tests (p.4).
Piecewise-linear approximation introduces bias; removing it costs speed (p.5).
Normal approximation via CLT holds only in the limit; the paper calls its use 'not necessarily unjustified' rather than proving it (p.5).
Review only: no worked simulation output; the emission-tomography example is deferred to another paper in the volume (p.2, p.6).
Equation bodies and figure images are absent from the text extraction, so eqs. 1-8 and the exponential/Poisson formulas are unverified here.
No empirical validation, error analysis or comparison of samplers is reported.
references_of_note: Stigler, S.M. (2002) Statistics on the Table, Harvard UP, pp.141-156 (ref 3): history of the t-test and related simulation. Background only; not about networks, lobbying, elections, persuasion, legislators or text measurement.
L'Ecuyer & Simard (2007) TestU01, ACM TOMS 33(4) (ref 7): empirical testing of RNGs. Relevant only to randomness quality.
Press et al. (1992) Numerical Recipes in C, 2nd ed., pp.288-290 (ref 13): sampling routines the paper recommends for normal and Poisson draws.
Burger & Starbird (2005) The Heart of Mathematics, p.546 (ref 1): source of the opening question on randomness. Not substantive.
Mersenne Twister RNG (ref 9; URL only, no author listed): the paper's recommended generator.
No reference in the list bears on networks, lobbying, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement.

rel.summary_md:
Harrison (2010) is a short tutorial and history of Monte Carlo simulation. It has no data and runs no simulation. The history runs from Buffon's needle (an intersection probability of 2/pi gives an estimate of pi) through De Forest, Galton and Gosset to von Neumann and Ulam's neutron-shielding work. It then gives a generic recipe: define the model as probability density functions, sample from them repeatedly, and tally the statistics of interest. The paper covers pseudo-random generators (linear congruential generators are poor; it recommends Mersenne Twister), the inversion method, acceptance-rejection, biased table approximation, and normal and Poisson sampling. For the last two it advises using library routines. Its warnings matter most for Paul's systems: simulation gives no exact answers, it is only as good as its model and inputs, it is prone to bugs, and analytic alternatives should be considered first.

The paper is a textbook source, not evidence. It cannot validate any Melange or Terrier parameter. The Melange cascade engines follow the recipe directly: a Bernoulli edge draw u < p on the build_P kernel, a tally of A-coloured activations, and the mean over MC iterations. Terrier's uncertainty draws use the paper's inversion method for categorical cells. The system goes beyond the paper in three ways: it keys draws to individual edges to get common random numbers, it uses splitmix64 and PCG64 generators, and it checks MC stability across seeds. The paper covers none of these. Its main use here is as a caution. The kernel saturation constant 6 and the bystander scale of $400k are unestimated, so the paper's point that simulation is only as good as its inputs applies directly. Its advice to try analytic methods first also supports Paul's wish to test an analytic proxy such as Viral Centrality against the MC cascade. One gap shows up in the code: the scenario and frontier spreads are reported as point means with no Monte Carlo standard error. That finding is UNVERIFIED and rests on a search of four files.

bearings.paper_claim: A simulation follows three steps: model the system as PDFs, sample from them repeatedly, and tally the statistics of interest. Its drawbacks: no exact solutions, the result is only as good as the model and its inputs, and the code is prone to bugs. Analytic and experimental alternatives should be considered first.
bearings.paper_location: p.2 (Introduction; the three-step pattern); p.3 (Defining the Model)
bearings.system_side: The cascade fits the three-step pattern exactly. Each edge is a Bernoulli PDF with p = x/(x+6) from build_P. An edge fires when the splitmix64 draw keyed by (iteration, edge) is below p. The run tallies A-coloured activations and takes the mean over MC iterations (MC = 20 by default, 40 for scenarios). The inputs the paper warns about are unestimated here: the saturation constant 6, the bystander rule min(0.9, $/400k), and the 0.4 + 0.6 sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v) cross-party factor.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The recipe and the caveats are generic and apply to any MC design, so they carry over fully. They say nothing about whether the cascade parameters are right, which IC model to use, or whether MC = 20 is enough. The paper does not cover common random numbers or variance reduction. Read it as a warning about the inputs, not as support for the design.

bearings.paper_claim: Inversion method: draw u uniform on [0,1) and invert the CDF. This works for any distribution with an invertible CDF, discrete ones included. For the binary case, sampling u < p is equivalent.
bearings.paper_location: pp.4-5 (Inversion); p.3 (PDF must be non-negative and integrate to 1)
bearings.system_side: C0 and C3 draws give each (replicate, field, row) one PCG64 uniform. A binary cell is set when u < p. A categorical cell takes idx = count of cumulative thresholds at or below u, with codes ordered highest exposure first. That is inverse-CDF sampling. The four negative lean fields use 1 - u. The results feed P(top10) tallies and Welford moments.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The sampling mechanics transfer exactly, because the math is the same. Correct mechanics do not make the output correct: the draws are only as good as the imputation class probabilities. Their calibration (ECE on holdout) remains the open question, which is the paper's input-quality caveat. Independence across cells in C0 is a model assumption the paper does not address.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper reports no error analysis, convergence diagnostics or comparison of samplers. On randomness quality it says only that LCGs fail standard tests and that Mersenne Twister passes most of them.
bearings.system_side: mc_stability_check.py reruns the topic frontier at MC = 100 and with SEED values 1 and 13. It compares the picked seed sets by Jaccard overlap, prefix agreement and spread delta. Bystander rolls use Python random, which is Mersenne Twister, the paper's recommended generator. Edge draws use splitmix64, which the paper does not discuss.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Here the system goes further than the source. The paper can endorse the choice of generator but supplies no criterion for MC budget or stability. Bars such as ROBUST at top-20 overlap >= 18 have to come from elsewhere, for example Almazaydeh et al. 2026, which the script itself cites.

bearings.paper_claim: Monte Carlo is a tool for analytically intractable problems. Where analytic alternatives exist they should be considered first, and simulation can be overused as a shortcut.
bearings.system_side: The scenario runner reruns the competitive cascade at MC = 40 under CRN for money, defection and stance moves. The sibling flip and break-even calculations are already closed-form: pflip = a/(a+b), and the break-even solves a(CU)/(a(CU)+b(comp)) = pfbase. Simulation is used only where the cascade has no closed form.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The split between analytic flip and break-even calculations and MC spread fits the paper's advice. The paper offers nothing on which analytic proxy, such as Viral Centrality or Katz-Bonacich, might replace the cascade MC. That comparison would need its own test.

gaps_exposed: Scenario, coalition and frontier spreads are returned as point means (tot/MC) with no Monte Carlo standard error or interval. The paper's warning that simulation gives no exact answers implies these figures should carry an MC error. UNVERIFIED: based on a search of scenario.py, budget_frontier.py, per_topic_coalition.py and mc_stability_check.py only.

Nobody has compared the cascade MC with an analytic proxy (Viral Centrality, or using the kb_benchmark Katz-Bonacich as a predictor of spread). The paper's advice to try analytic methods first points to this comparison, and Paul's Fink note asks for it.
The kernel inputs (saturation constant 6, bystander scale $400k, cross-party factor) are unestimated. The paper says the output is only as good as these inputs, and nothing validates them.
Terrier's draws assume that imputation class probabilities are calibrated. Draws by inversion from miscalibrated probabilities would be exact samples from the wrong PDF.
flags: Paul's annotation entry for this cluster names Raychaudhuri 2008 (WSC), not Harrison 2010, and it is empty: no takeaways, system links or anchor. Harrison's markup is in the extraction but has no annotation note. The 'Raychaudhuri 2008 / Harrison 2010' citation pairing in the component positions treats them as one entry, so the two papers should not be conflated.
The paper cannot validate the MC = 20 or MC = 40 budgets, the CRN design or any cascade parameter. Calling it support for the competitive cascade would overstate it.
No conflict found with D-025, D-021 or D-104..D-108, and the paper argues for neither of the rejected SNA proposals.
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence agrees with Paul's position, but only weakly. Paul treats Monte Carlo as a tool, and the paper says the same. His highlights (the three-step pattern, the green highlight on the key points for defining a model, the point that input density limits accuracy, and the advice to use library functions) fit how the system is built. Python's Mersenne Twister generates the bystander draws, the cascade follows sample-and-tally, and Terrier uses inversion. His Fink note asks for something cheaper than Monte Carlo, and the paper's advice to try analytic methods first supports it. The system went with MC plus CRN and has not tested an analytic proxy, so that request is still open. His annotation record is stale in a different way: the Raychaudhuri/Harrison entry has no takeaways, so his notes do not record that the built cascade uses edge-keyed splitmix64 common random numbers, which neither tutorial covers.

related.why: Weimer uses Monte Carlo as a negative control, an applied validation use of the generic sampling-and-tallying technique Harrison describes. Paul highlighted it.
It supplies the MC-budget noise evidence (CELF++ at 50 simulations) that motivates mc_stability_check.py, the error analysis Harrison leaves out.
It defines the competitive IC model whose spread the cascade estimates by the Monte Carlo recipe Harrison describes.
IC spread estimation is the costly MC step whose cost Harrison flags as a drawback, and efficient IM methods aim to reduce it.
